projectOutComesReport:
Australia is a major hot-spot of global biomass burning emissions, but wildfires in this region are less well-studied compared to other (i.e., US) biomes. This RAPID project supported observations of volatile organic compounds (VOCs) in Australia during the historic 2019/2020 wildfire season, colloquially called the ?Black Summer?. Field observations are used to improve our understanding of the role of fuel type, combustion conditions, and photochemical processes on the abundance and speciation of VOCs present in wildfire plumes.

A proton-transfer-reaction time-of-flight mass spectrometer (PTR-TOF-MS) was deployed to New South Wales, Australia during the COALA-2020 (Characterizing Organics and Aerosol Loading over Australia) field campaign. Back-trajectory analysis suggests that the smoke plume intersecting our site originated from fires burning near the coast of the New South Wales/Victoria border, approximately 390 km south of site. Because the fuel load in this region is primarily eucalyptus, the smoke was expected to have different characteristics than smoke in US fires.

As the plume had travelled ~8 hrs before reaching the site, we restrict our analysis to VOC species that would be minimally impacted by plume chemistry during the overnight plume transport. This leaves 15 compounds for which we examine emission factors, includes 6 compounds previously not reported for this compound, and acrolein, which has significant health impacts. We compare our derived emission factors with those from previous studies in New South Wales, Australia, western U.S. wildfires, and lab-based studies. We see unexpectedly good agreement across these biomes. A major finding is that emissions factors from non-Australian studies can effectively be used in air quality models if they?re derived from analogous but geographically separated biomes.

Finally, we examined the increase in VOC-related OH reactivity that results from long-range plume transport. OH reactivity quantifies the total amount of reactive carbon in the atmosphere. We saw OH reactivity was significantly elevated above ?typical? levels in the plume as a result of elevated levels of furans, alkenes, and aromatics, with smaller enhancements from oxygenated non-aromatic compounds. The OH reactivity this plume brought to the site nearly doubled that of the reactivity resulting from biogenic isoprene and monoterpenes at the site, suggesting large contributions to next-day ozone formation from transported VOCs.

To date, the VOC data acquired through this project has been foundational to two peer-reviewed publications. The dataset is publicly available, and expected to be used in broader future studies. Additionally, this work supported the training and education of one graduate student, and fostered new international collaboration in the atmospheric chemistry community.

abstractText:
Climate is an important factor in determining why plants and animals live where they do. When climate shifts, we anticipate that plants and animals may be forced to track their preferred climates across the landscape. Identifying the extent to which plants and animals will respond to changing climate is one of the most pressing questions in ecology and conservation biology today. To meet this challenge, this project will examine past responses to environmental change on both the continental scale and at the site level. The core of the outreach activities will bring the fossil discovery experience to students and the public while demonstrating the effects of climate change on ecological systems. These opportunities will reach people from across the broader Atlanta community, in addition to East African undergraduate students who participate in workshops facilitated by the Conservation Paleobiology in Africa program. 

This research will estimate the ‘climate fidelity’ that individual mammal and plant biomes have exhibited since the last glaciation. It will calculate the extent to which observed changes in the climates that plants and animals occupy correspond with the climates of urban and agricultural regions, creating a ‘human tolerance index.’ Using these methods, it will demonstrate how much climate drives range determination across trophic levels by comparing the relative fidelity of plants versus animals. By examining ecosystem responses to a major drought at Natural Trap Cave, Wyoming, researchers can test hypotheses about long-term ecosystem responses to precipitation while validating predicted species-level climate responses. By understanding how species respond to changing climate, we can identify which species and strategies to prioritize in order to conserve biodiversity going forward.

abstractText:
Process Systems Engineering (PSE) has historically been advanced by using physics-based mathematical models and computer algorithms to design, optimize and control complex systems. Recent advances in the broad field of Data Science and Artificial Intelligence have led to a series of breakthroughs in the development of Machine Learning (ML) tools that can be used to derive mathematical models from large data sets. However, ML-based models can be limited in their ability to give insight into the physical origins of the system’s behavior and can result in poor predictions outside of the range of the original data set used to create the model. This CAREER project aims to develop hybrid modeling approaches that preserve what we already know about system behavior to make data-driven ML models more reliable leading to more accurate medical diagnoses, smarter autonomous vehicles, and safer chemical plants. Curriculum development activities are proposed aimed at introducing data science concepts into Chemical Engineering courses and high school statistics classes. Proposed outreach activities are aimed at increasing the number of female engineers in the field of PSE.

The proposed methodology aims at developing algorithms that will enable the simultaneous training of modern ML models (i.e., Neural Networks and Gaussian Process Models) with physical constraints that are derived from discretization of first-principles based models. The proposed research will involve a systematic study of pre-processing and integration of data, identification of low-dimensional descriptive feature spaces, hybridization of ML models with first-principles based models and quantification of the uncertainty of hybrid model predictions. The specific research aims are: (1) Theoretically advancing mathematical techniques for training nonparametric ML models to satisfy first-principles based model predictions (hybrid modeling); (2) Quantification of the uncertainty of hybrid models in the presence of noisy and incomplete data sets; (3) Algorithmic development for mixed-integer nonlinear optimization problems for design and synthesis with embedded hybrid models. A series of case studies that include production of pharmaceuticals, polymers and chemicals will be used to develop a benchmarking library for testing various hybrid modeling architectures. The design and optimization of bioprocesses will be studied using hybrid modeling to connect gene-level control to macroscale process optimization. A set of hybrid modeling and optimization teaching modules, suitable for incorporation within existing core courses of the Chemical Engineering curriculum, will be developed and broadly disseminated. Outreach activities are proposed that are aimed at introducing data-driven decision-making to high-school students through statistics classes and increasing gender diversity in the field of PSE. A high-school teacher will be hosted by the Principal Investigator in collaboration with the Center for Education Integrating Science, Mathematics, and Computing (CEISMC)at Georgia Tech and the Georgia Intern Fellowships for Teachers (GIFT) program, which provides paid summer STEM internships in industry workplaces and University laboratories for K-12 science, mathematics, and technology teachers.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

projectOutComesReport:
Introduction: The chemical engineering community increasingly recognizes both the potential and risks of using black-box, data-driven methods for decision-making. This NSF CAREER project aimed to support a responsible transition to a data-driven future, by developing engineering-informed machine learning (ML) (or hybrid models) that integrate data with first-principles to improve reliability, interpretability, and performance.

Achieving this integration posed significant mathematical challenges. It required opening the black boxes of ML and integrating them with optimization theory and engineering constraints. These challenges are particularly relevant in systems like chemical manufacturing, bioprocessing, carbon capture, and power grids, where engineers must either rely on costly simulations, or work with limited mechanistic understanding and sparse data.

This project developed hybrid, predictive, and computationally efficient tools to bridge these gaps. It also helped train a new generation of researchers at the intersection of chemical engineering and data science. In addition to advancing theoretical foundations, this work transformed how data science is practiced and taught in chemical engineering, produced open-source tools adopted by the broader community, and contributed to sustainable, resilient technological solutions.


Intellectual Merit - Key Scientific Contributions: This research made foundational contributions to process systems engineering by combining modern machine learning with engineering models and optimization theory. Major intellectual advances include:

  1. Hybrid Modeling: Hybrid modeling techniques were developed combining physics-based models with ML algorithms, resulting in models that are more reliable, especially when experimental data are sparse/noisy. This allows engineers to make better predictions with fewer resources. In an invited article, three approaches for hybridization were employed for a chemical reaction process (i.e., Physics-informed ML, model calibration, and hybrid modeling) bringing together many fields and identifying critical challenges, future directions, and collaboration opportunities.
  2. Model identification using hybrid methods: A new model identification method was introduced based on Neural Ordinary Differential Equations that improves the calibration of process dynamics from limited experimental data. Dynamic model identification for complex systems is critical for enabling process design and control. This approach was applied to calibrate bioprocess reactor systems and stiff microkinetic systems.
  3. Optimization with hybrid models: Novel optimization algorithms using various fidelities of models and machine learning surrogates were developed. Published research demonstrated that integrating hybrid models within mathematical optimization frameworks enables faster and more reliable solutions to challenging problems. For example, this approach improved the safe and reliable operation of electric power grids under contingency scenarios, which is critically important for grid resilience and national security. It was also employed in designing an adsorption-based carbon capture system, leading to new design and operating solutions that competing solvers could not locate.
  4. New global optimization methods with underestimations of hybrid models: Novel data-driven global optimization algorithms were proposed and benchmarked that construct convex underestimators of multifidelity data. These methods reduce reliance on exact or unknown functional forms. Overall, this work led to both mathematical proofs and practical solutions for different classes of simulation-based optimization problems.

Broader Impacts: Beyond theoretical contributions, this project addressed pressing challenges at the intersection of sustainability, energy, and responsible ML. This project has supported high school, undergraduate, and graduate students, preparing a new generation of chemical engineers skilled in data science.  Key activities include: 

  1. Increasing interpretability in ML: By embedding engineering knowledge into ML models, we improve robustness and transparency. This is especially important in critical applications (such as chemical manufacturing, biomanufacturing, or power grid optimization) where black-box models can lead to incorrect predictions and pose risks.
  2. Energy Security: Our hybrid modeling frameworks were applied to optimize power grid operations under contingency scenarios, ensuring safer and more reliable electricity supply and supporting national energy security and resilience.
  3. Decarbonization: Our hybrid optimization models were used to improve the design of CO₂ capture systems, making them more efficient and cost-effective. 
  4. Open-Source Software: We released our tools on GitHub, which has already been adopted by other research groups, extending the impact of our methods beyond our lab.
  5. New course and graduate program: The PI developed a new course on data-driven process systems engineering, now offered as part of an online graduate certificate taken by students and professionals from major industries. The certificate received Georgia Tech’s Curriculum Innovation Award and AIChE’s David Himmelblau Award for Innovations in Computer-Based Chemical Engineering Education. This curriculum has reached approximately 120 undergraduates, 90 graduate students, and 20 industry professionals. Many students have secured careers as data scientists in the chemical process industries and course material is available online and has served as a model for others.
  6. Dissemination: The work was published in peer-reviewed journals and presented at numerous national and international conferences, including invited keynote talks advocating for the safe adoption and hybridization of ML with engineering principles.
  7. Outreach: The PI and her team hosted and mentored high school students during the summer and participated in STEAM workshops at local Atlanta elementary schools.

abstractText:
Understanding the emergence and spread of disease-causing parasites is an essential goal of evolutionary biology. It is well recognized that dispersal in space can provide protection for hosts against infection, however many organisms can also disperse in time through the process of dormancy. Dormancy reflects the ability of an individual to enter a reversible state of reduced metabolic activity. It is a strategy that has evolved numerous times across the tree of life, but is particularly prevalent among microorganisms. While it is well known that dormancy allows populations to persist in the face of harsh environmental conditions like thermal stress and starvation, far less is known about whether dormancy can provide protection against infection by parasites. This project will advance multiple fields of biology through the integration of mathematical theory, laboratory evolution experiments, and bioinformatic analysis of genomic data collected from a range of ecosystems around the world. The project will engage elementary students and the public through a combination of K-5 classroom activities and an exhibit in a public science festival. Educational impacts include immersing students from diverse ages and backgrounds in teaching modules and research experiences that use physical and computer models to emphasize the scale and nature of microbial interactions.

The central premise of the research project is that dormancy is an important life-history strategy that modifies the evolutionary ecology of host-parasite interactions. The project addresses this premise, first, by developing theory to assess how fluctuations caused by host-parasite dynamics influence the emergence and maintenance of dormancy beyond classical expectations. Second, experimental evolution trials with a bacteria-virus (i.e., phage) system will be used to test predictions about how the preservation of genetic and phenotypic diversity in dormant pools (i.e., seed banks) affects the rate and mode of host-parasite coevolution. Finally, a combination of informatics and direct molecular manipulation will be used to test the ability of parasites to overcome a dormancy refuge by modifying host behavior via a novel arms-race strategy. Bridging major themes in life history and population biology, the research will advance the study of dormancy and how it alters the long-term ecology and evolution of host-parasite interactions.

projectOutComesReport:
Overview:. Viruses and bacteria interact, leading to the coevolution of bacterial defense and phage counter-defense. This study explored bacterial persistence in the face of viral infections and emergent phage-bacteria coexistence through analysis of the role of seed banks as a host refuge from infection. In doing so, the study addressed three major objectives: (i) Assessing how fluctuations in resource availability influences and maintains dormancy; (ii) Testing predictions of how seed banks change the rate of mode of phage-bacteria coevolution; (iii) Developing models to explore how bacterial dormancy impacts the propagation of phage. By combining theory, models, and experiments, this study found evidence for the evolutionary benefits of dormancy, dormancy’s role in buffering fluctuations induced by viral lysis, and novel spatial phenomena in which phage expansion is slowed as bacteria initiate dormancy in spatially explicit habitats thereby evading phage infection and lysis.

Intellectual Merit: First, the project explored the evolutionary benefits of dormancy as a form of bet hedging by incorporating the physiologically realistic process of dormancy initiation. A combination of models and theory revealed that the benefits of bet hedging are diminished in the face of delays to the onset of dormancy. Nonetheless, optimal strategies exist and are linked to the switching frequencies in stochastic simulations of fluctuating environments. Second, in vitro experiments showed that the eco-evolutionary dynamics of phage and bacteria are buffered by the presence of a seed bank which reduces the ability of phage to lyse present bacterial populations. Finally, a combination of theory, simulations and bacteria were used to explore the impact of dormancy on phage expansions in spatially explicit bacterial populations. Observations that spatially expanding phage infections stopped early when infecting sporulating bacteria vs. bacteria that did not sporulate suggest that dormancy can provide a refuge in the near-term with the caveat that some phage may continue to persist as ‘virospores’. These results suggest that both phage and bacteria can leverage refuges over multiple time scales, reducing the intensity of infections in the short term but potentially extending interactions in the long-term.

Broader Impacts: This project provided use cases and educational materials for multiple international, student workshops, including an online, two-day workshop on epidemic dynamics (Spring 2020 & Spring 2021), an in-person week-long workshop on virus dynamics across scales (Spring 2022) and two follow-up week-long workshops on phage-bacteria dynamics across scales (Summer 2024 and Summer 2025. Overall, these activities directly impacted more than 150 early career trainees. Multiple PhD students contributed to pedagogical course development including the release of ‘Quantitative Biosciences: Dynamics Across Cells, Organisms, and Populations’ and computational companions in Python, R, and MATLAB. Two PhD students, one postdoc, and multiple visiting students were supported as part of this proposal.

abstractText:
The broader impact/commercial potential of this I-Corps project is the development of a software tool for polymer selection, design and discovery. Potential customers of this technology include polymer chemists or materials designers in companies that manufacture or utilize polymers in industries such as auto, chemicals, and oil and gas.  The value of this technology lies in overcoming the traditional, laborious and expensive trial-and-error approaches to materials development. The total R&D expenditure of the polymer manufacturing industry is about $10 billion per year. This technology has the potential to save an estimated savings of $100 million per year.  In addition, the acceleration of product design workflows could dramatically shorten time-to-market for products that must undergo evolutionary changes throughout the product’s life-cycle.

This I-Corps project is based on the development of a data-driven machine learning tool to achieve accelerated application-specific polymer design and development. Machine learning (ML) algorithms trained on an underlying database produce predictive models, which can 1) make instantaneous predictions of properties of a new yet-to-be-synthesized polymer, and 2) make recommendations of new and existing polymers that will meet design objectives. The goal is to create a customized application-specific polymer design tool for end-user companies, and a generic data-to-model product line that ingests in-house proprietary (legacy/historic) polymer data to produce predictive models for polymer manufacturing companies.

projectOutComesReport:
Over the years, the Ramprasad Group at Georgia Tech has developed IP and innovations in Polymer Informatics, that can accelerate the development, design and optimization of polymers and formulations for a variety of applications. Our NSF I-Corps team sought to determine the market value of our technology, including the identification of target customer segments, validation and quantification of the value proposition, and the determination of product-market fit for data-driven machine learning based polymer property prediction and polymer design software. To gain insights into these three criteria, our team conducted over 100 customer discovery interviews within the US and overseas with professionals working at various points in the value chain of polymer products.

Three major customer segments emerged from these efforts: polymer synthesizers, formulators, and product developers. Synthesizers are scientists involved in creating novel polymer structures on a day-to-day basis. Example companies under this category would be Solvay Specialty Polymers, SABIC, Dow. Formulators are generally involved in taking existing polymers and chemicals, mixing, and reacting them in new ratios that create materials with unique properties. Example companies our team talked to were Henkel, Bosch, Proctor & Gamble. Lastly, product developers are individuals that purchase existing polymer products for applications in assembled goods. Example companies that fall in this category include Apple, Kimberly-Clark, Toyota. The team achieved the hundred interview target mark by attending three different trade shows (including Specialty Chemical America in Fort Worth, the Polyolefins Trade show in Houston, and the advance electronics manufacturing tradeshow in San Diego). In addition, trips were taken to Los Angeles and San Jose area within the US, as well as to UK, Germany, and South Korea to interview relevant companies. Some of the most recognizable companies that participated in the customer discovery process include Tesla/Space-X, Apple, Solvay Specialty Polymers, ExxonMobil, BASF, Henkel, Northrop Grumman, and Kimberly-Clark Corporation.

Several critical and tangible outcomes have emerged from our effort, thanks to the NSF I-Corps program. One of them is the segmentation of the market such that companies within a given segment have common goals and pain points. A couple of examples of segments include polymers/plastics for packaging, and polymers for electronics & electrical applications (devices, batteries, fuel cells). Likewise, on the Technology Development side, we have learned that, while there is general excitement in using ML methods to accelerate materials development, clients are at different stages of readiness. The common problem is that in-house datasets are in various levels of cleanliness and organization. Data curation and data analysis are thus bottlenecks that client companies need assistance with. In addition, most client companies go beyond polymer chemistry in their development work; process and environmental conditions are critical and must be inserted into the ML pipeline.

Perhaps the most tangible outcome of this effort is the formation of the startup company, Matmerize, Inc., (https://www.matmerize.com) based on the lessons learned from this I-Corps program. Matmerize is actively engaging with several clients, and has created a cloud-based materials design software, called PolymRize?. This cloud-based machine learning software can be securely accessed by polymer and formulations chemists via a web browser. It utilizes Matmerize-proprietary or client-proprietary data to build models that can instantly predict the properties and aids in the rapid design of new yet-to-be-synthesized polymers and formulations. Matmerize seeks to define the new industry standard for cost-effective accelerated polymer materials and formulation development by eliminating expensive and long trial-and-error cycles. Companies are beginning to realize the value and opportunity presented by leveraging materials data. Matmerize seeks to take the logical next, but a transformative, step ? leveraging the data to extract knowledge and guide the next experiments toward cost-effective and intelligent materials design.

title: I-Corps: Using machine learning methods and polymer data to predict properties of new polymers and accelerate application-specific polymer design

abstractText:
The long-term goal of the proposed research is to understand, manage efficiently, and utilize dynamical mechanisms like propagation on large networks, occurring across natural, social, and technological systems. Understanding such processes enables us to manipulate them for our benefit. Propagation and networks have numerous applications in areas as diverse as public health and epidemiology, systems biology, cyber security, viral marketing and social media---hence progress in this domain promises scientific, commercial and social benefits. The proposed research aims to develop extensible, data-driven frameworks for propagation-related problems getting more implementable and generalizable tools. The PI's investigations will lead to novel mining and learning problems and scalable techniques which can be applied to massive datasets, helping make more informed choices for future. Educational activities are also closely integrated with this research agenda, including integrating research with education through courses, tutorials, and other university programs. 

Most current work in propagation mining assume the existence of well-calibrated models. Performing model calibration is typically very expensive, and not robust. Indeed, in many situations it is not clear which parameterized model should be calibrated. However there is an increasing availability of surveillance data like online media and medical health records.  The PI's approach is unique in the sense that the aim is to directly use surveillance data and formulate optimization problems based on the data and network together. The proposed problems include inventing data-driven immunization policies for diseases like influenza, automatically finding missing infections/activations in cascade datasets, and automatically learning graph summaries based on distributed feature representations of propagation data as well as the network. The PI proposes to develop a flexible and expressive framework for all these problems. In addition, the developed algorithms will be applied to various domains, leveraging multiple collaborations.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

projectOutComesReport:
Overview: This project advanced the scientific understanding of how information, influence, and disease propagate across large, complex networks. As it happened, the project unfolded during a time of historic urgency: the COVID-19 pandemic. Hence the research turned out to be especially timely, anticipating the growing need for integrated data-driven and model-based approaches to public health crises. By combining AI, machine learning, algorithm design, and epidemiological modeling, the research developed new methods for analyzing and forecasting dynamical processes - like the spread of disease or failures in infrastructure - using real-time data and scalable computational tools.

Through these efforts, the project delivered novel methodological contributions, advancing both the frontiers of artificial intelligence and practical public health modeling. The research team’s algorithms became part of the official CDC COVID-19 Forecast Hub, where they consistently ranked among the top five performing models across multiple evaluation cycles. The project also resulted in over 30 peer-reviewed publications at premier venues, new software tools, public datasets, and widespread dissemination through courses, workshops, and invited talks.

Intellectual Merit: This research bridged the theoretical and practical divide between data-driven machine learning models and mechanistic models used in public health and infrastructure systems. Key contributions included:

- Deep Learning for Epidemic Forecasting: development of state-of-the-art neural models for epidemic forecasting and their integration in real time pandemic forecasting.

- Differentiable Agent-Based Models (GradABM, NeurABM and EINNs): Enabling end-to-end learning with epidemiological simulators, connecting them with rich datasets. This work merges domain and data-driven insights for healthcare modeling.

- Decision-Focused Learning (SO-EBM): Optimization-aware learning under uncertainty.

- Hypergraph and Subgraph Models: Enhanced representation of group-level interactions in disease spread.

- Time Series Generalization (FOIL) and Multimodal Forecasting (Time-MMD): Addressing robustness and complexity in real-world forecasts.

Broader Impacts: Beyond technical contributions, the project made substantial societal and educational impacts:

- Public Health Forecasting at Scale: Supported CDC and other (campus level, hospital level) efforts in real-time response to a once-in-century pandemic. 

- Interdisciplinary Education: Created and taught a novel 'Data Science for Epidemiology' course. Engaged students from different backgrounds through REUs and outreach.

- Community Building: Launched the epiDAMIK workshop series at major conferences. Also gave multiple tutorials at high profile venues. 

- Open Science: Released software libraries and datasets for community use.

- National Recognition: Invited talks at NAE, award-winning publications, and student honors.

Conclusion: This CAREER project produced a rich set of scientific innovations, practical tools, and educational resources that are shaping how we understand and respond to the dynamics of epidemics, infrastructure failures, and other large-scale network phenomena. The outcomes reflect the power of integrating domain expertise, algorithmic rigor, and real-world data to address critical and urgent societal challenges. The project’s legacy continues through ongoing collaborations, extended modeling platforms, and a growing community of trained students and researchers committed to data-driven, scientifically grounded public health and systems analysis.

abstractText:
This research will design, develop, and evaluate novel smartphone applications that help youth explore and leverage their social networks to engage in collective action, and assess the impact of this action.  From affiliation with social movements through the use of Twitter hashtags, to collective organizing through Facebook, social computing tools have catalyzed new and exciting forms of civic engagement (efforts taken by individuals and collectives to address issues of societal concern). While historically it has been challenging to engage youth in civic action, social computing platforms offer a media-relevant way for youth to address issues that matter to them. However, despite increased opportunities for civic engagement online, youth can have difficulty navigating their social networks, which creates challenges for understanding and putting to use the social capital within networks, that is, the beneficial resources that can support collective action. This research examines how interactive visualizations of youth's social networks can help youth more effectively understand and put to use the social capital within their networks. Such visualizations may support civic engagement by easing access to the rich and complex information about social ties, helping youth evaluate the impact they have through online civic action, preparing them to make effective decisions about future activities.
 
The work will include the design, development, and evaluation of two novel smartphone applications. Although there is a large literature on how best to visualize these networks from an algorithmic perspective, very little is known about how people, especially young people, interpret network visualizations, nor whether or when network visualizations may enhance access to and utilization of social capital. This project will contribute new empirical findings and novel software tools to fill this research gap. Additionally, although complex network data is increasingly packaged for public consumption, there are few standards for how to do so effectively, particularly in the context of mobile visualizations where small screen real estate dramatically amplifies the visualization challenge. The research will contribute new knowledge regarding how best to visualize network data for lay audiences, on the mobile platforms that people are increasingly using to interact with data. This work will yield empirical assessments of how designed interfaces can best manage the complexities of networked data in order to amplify cognition, action, and feelings of empowerment. This work will culminate in a conceptual framework to guide the design of social computing tools for youth civic engagement.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

projectOutComesReport:
This project has contributed research towards understanding how social computing tools can 1) empower youth to engage in social action that uplifts their communities, and 2) help build resilience within marginalized communities during times of crisis. First, through a series of qualitative and design-based empirical studies, this work produced new empirical knowledge detailing how youth activists use social media for community organizing and the challenges therein. Using findings from qualitative and participatory design studies, we designed and built of a software application called the SwagApp. This software utilizes the Twitter API to visualize youth activists’ online social networks and create an online collaborative space through which activists can work as a team to strategically engage their social networks for community organizing. There are a growing number of commercially-available applications that help businesses, governments and other organizations to manage their social media accounts, and connect to their customers. However, while social media platforms are often touted as systems that enable voices to be heard, there is little scientific knowledge available regarding how technology can support the work of grassroots initiatives specifically by helping activists to visualize, reason about, and act upon information about social networks. Our empirical findings and the design and development of the SwagApp addresses this knowledge gap, and help inform researchers and industry practitioners regarding how such tools can be best designed, particularly in the context of supporting youth activism.

This research has produced several papers published at leading human-computer interaction (HCI) venues (e.g., ACM CSCW and ACM CHI). These publications provide insights into how social computing tools can empower youth towards social action. Much prior HCI research on wellbeing has explored how technology can be designed to support individual level behavioral change. Our work took a different approach, by examining how technology (e.g., interactive network visualizations) can empower communities to better effect positive societal change. With this focus, our research contributes to HCI but also public health, as it demonstrates how technology can help communities engage in social action that addresses social factors at the neighborhood and societal level—influences that act as barriers to wellbeing. Specifically, our work demonstrates the role that technology can play in addressing fundamental social determinants of health, that is, the conditions in which we live and work that impact wellbeing. 

Through a nationwide survey with high school-aged youth, this project has also produced new knowledge regarding the role of social media for facilitating and hindering youth’s critical consciousness, that is, the awareness, motivation, and actions taken to combat societal inequities. In particular, our findings characterized how the political content, critical discourse, content moderation policies, and recommender systems on various social media platforms may motivate and demotivate youth to learn about and take action against sociopolitical issues. As such, this work contributes to understanding the ways in which social media promotes and hinders critical consciousness development among youth. Particularly, this work expands upon prior work to shed light on how youth not only appropriate social media to disseminate information and organize for political purposes, but also how youth may be learning about sociopolitical issues and responding to calls to social action through these platforms.

In an additional study within this project, we investigated the role of information and communication technologies in maintaining community and providing care for youth activists during a time of crisis. Through interviews with youth activists and staff at community organizations during the COVID-19 pandemic, we contribute findings that characterize the nuances of care within youth empowerment programs and the sociotechnical challenges therein. Building upon previous HCI and CSCW literature on youth development and theories of care, this study characterized how youth empowerment programs are organizations rich in caring behaviors for supporting youth, and how caring for youth over computer-mediated communication was especially difficult amidst the pandemic. These findings contribute to an understanding of breakdowns in care over ​​computer-mediated communication during community stressors, when key aspects of care are not supported in the design of information and communication technologies. Additionally, this work contributes a set of opportunities for future innovation to better care for youth during moments of crisis. 

Finally, this project contributed new educational resources and student mentorship opportunities. These include research opportunities for undergraduate and graduate students that have taught them HCI research skills, the development of educational curriculum including a digital health equity course for university students and a network literacy toolkit for youth, and the use of findings from this work in invited seminar talks at various universities to further enrich student education.

abstractText:
Stem cell research has been marked by scientific, ethical, and juridical concerns for nearly two decades. Additionally, stem cell therapy has wide-ranging implications for medical practice and for the future of bioscience, but important cultural differences in clinics and labs remain under-analyzed. This project focuses on the rise of stem cell research and epistemic cultures in three different labs that translate stem cell research into frontier science and stem cell therapies as they shift towards a market-oriented political culture of commercialization. The three labs to be investigated differ in terms of their transnational funding and networks, their standards for evidence-controlled experiments, their verification by the larger scientific community, and their level of commercialization. Instead of analyzing stem cell research through the lens of the nation-state, this project focuses on cultural differences of stem cell science within a nation. It thus investigates a broad range of settings that make knowledge production and circulation possible in stem cell research. 

This project investigates the mechanics of knowledge production in three laboratories in the context of the shift towards market-oriented political culture of science. It has two main objectives: (1) Investigation of differences in the epistemic cultures of stem cell research at the three laboratories by exploring differences in the deployment of literary, social, and material technologies in the production of scientific knowledge. It explores whether and how differences in the mechanics of knowledge production explain the differing epistemological and social responses towards the epistemic things produced at these three laboratories. (2) Investigation of the impact of the shifting market-oriented political culture of science on the three stem cell laboratories. The project, thus, explores: (a) how political culture has impacted the practices of the three laboratories, and (b) whether and how the national and international networks of the laboratories have led to differential impact on the credibility of the scientific practices at those laboratories despite their being located within the same regulatory regime.

projectOutComesReport:
The project shows how political and epistemic cultures of stem cell science in India have been differentially impacted because of national and international location. Stem cell research and therapy in India had started with the objective of making India "a global hub for stem cell research." However, proliferation of stem cell therapy clinics and resulting international criticisms made stem cell research and therapy in India a site of geopolitical friction, which resulted in continual changes in national policy and impacted epistemic cultures of stem cell labs/clinics. Nevertheless, as the project highlights through a study of three Indian stem cell research and therapy labs/clinics, the impact of location within a nation and internationally has been differential and was navigated differently, resulting in different technoscientific outcomes. The project found that ownership-status (public, private, or not-for-profit) did not matter much but the status of the clinic/lab within the national and international scientific community and among the policy makers played a significant role. Technoscientific practices at the government-owned hospital utilized the inescapable contingency in the translation between governmental rationality and the practice of government (that defines any national policy) and the reputation of the lead scientist to conduct cutting-edge cardiac related stem cell research and therapy. The not-for-profit clinic, on the other hand, used its organization as a boundary infrastructure, which had also resulted in several international collaborations, to further its eyecare related stem cell research and therapy and its findings continued to be well-received nationally and internationally. Moreover, both, the not-for-profit and the government-owned lab/clinic, navigated the international concerns by blaming clinics such as the private-owned one as the source of the problem. The private clinic, which was often criticized, internationally and nationally, for "selling a miracle," navigated the concerns by presenting its research and therapy not as outside science, but as the outside of the science - the frontier. This project, thus, shows how technoscience is practiced in the context of geopolitical frictions and how these frictions impact political and epistemic cultures of science(s) within a nation; the impact, nevertheless, is not same for all labs within the nation.

abstractText:
This project will advance research around using health-monitoring tools, such as sensor-based physical activity trackers, to support healthy behaviors for children in low-income families.  In comparison to the general population, low-income families face disproportionate barriers to wellness, such as persistent social stressors and limited environmental support for behavior change. As such, a key technical challenge is designing systems that help families learn how to overcome these barriers to physical activity. To identify design opportunities, the team will first study how lower-income families currently use and think about physical activity tracking devices and data. This knowledge will then be used to redesign an existing software application that motivates children to exercise by helping them learn from sensor-collected physical activity data.  In this research, the team will work closely with families to target the application more directly at their needs, while adding features to support "experiential learning"--the idea that reflecting on concrete past experiences can help people develop insights that guide their future behavior.  The researchers will then conduct long-term studies of the tool in use, evaluating its impact on exercise and health, while learning more about the design issues that arise when supporting family-based activity tracking and learning.  The combination of the use of experiential learning approaches, the low-income and family contexts, and the long-term evaluation all promise to extend what is currently known about designing systems that motivate physical activity.  This work will have a practical impact on the widespread public health problem of childhood obesity, both by directly helping the families involved in the project and indirectly helping others through releasing the experiential learning tools and new design insights.  The work will also provide educational benefits.  Apart from the health education aspects of the system itself, the team will develop learning opportunities where college students work closely with local communities both to improve their learning and help those communities.  These opportunities will also give lower-income children a way to participate directly in computer science research, helping them see what it would be like to be computer scientists or researchers themselves.
 
In the first stage of work, the project will develop a grounded theory of how well existing physical activity tracking tools do and could support data collection, management, and experiential learning in low-income families. This theory will be developed through a combination of interviews and a trial deployment of activity trackers to both children and their caregivers.  This theory will guide the second stage, in which the team will conduct participatory design research with families. Through this work, the team will design, build, and evaluate system prototypes that emphasize elements of experiential learning, particularly abstract conceptualization (identifying meaningful insights from activity data that can be applied to future situations) and active experimentation (testing out these new insights).  The second stage will have two main outcomes. The first outcome will be a high-fidelity prototype of a system that tracks and represents physical activity among family members in a way that engages their attention and helps them engage in collaborative learning and experimentation. The second outcome will be a framework for the design of experiential learning systems that builds on the theory from the first stage.  The prototype will be the basis of the third stage, a six-month deployment of the system to a number of families.  In this stage, the team will gradually deploy features of the full system, and use a combination of survey instruments, interviews, and logged activity and usage data to refine the design framework and to evaluate the system's effect on knowledge, attitudes, and behaviors around physical activity. In total, the work will lead to design recommendations that will help researchers and developers build persuasive systems that encourage active engagement with physical activity data. In addition, this work will produce protocols for evaluating systems that support experiential learning from health data, knowledge about the challenges of designing such systems for families rather than individuals, and the software system itself. Each of these outputs will be valuable to both researchers and designers in this domain.  Furthermore, the participatory design workshops will engage lower-income children in the creative process of technology design, which can pique their interest in a computer science career, while also providing the context for an innovative service-learning curriculum for existing college students.  Finally, the software system will help to educate families about simple biological principles about the importance of physical activity in a socially and socioeconomically relevant way.

projectOutComesReport:
This project investigated how mobile technologies can help low-socioeconomic (low-SES) families overcome barriers to wellbeing by deriving meaningful insights from sensor-collected data about their physical activity. Through the iterative design and evaluation of two mobile health (mHealth) applications, this project has made design, empirical, and theoretical contributions to the fields of human-computer interaction, social computing, and digital health.

We began with a mixed-method formative study assessing practices around and attitudes towards sensor-collected physical activity data (e.g., step count data) in low-SES families. Our findings characterized how physical activity tracking wristbands support families' awareness of their activity levels, but also how these devices fall short of enabling the full experiential learning process (e.g., helping families draw out insights from this data that can be applied in the future). 

Based on these findings, we conducted several studies and participatory design activities with families, children?s story writers, and additional stakeholders to iteratively develop Storywell, a mobile application that uses narrative to support experiential learning from health data in families. In Storywell, caregivers (e.g., parents) and their children monitor physical activity levels through wearable activity trackers, visualize progress towards activity goals, and unlock interactive digital storybook chapters when goals are met. These stories have embedded physical activity themes and reflection prompts designed to help families learn from their activity data and past experiences and develop positive health values. Through a study evaluating Storywell with families, we characterized how a sense of connectedness manifested when caregivers used the app with their children, how these feelings nurtured engagement with Storywell, and how designing for connectedness is an important design approach for future family health technologies.

We developed a second version of the app, Storywell 2, to investigate the value of connecting families in low-SES neighborhoods to one another in mHealth apps. This new version introduced features that allow families to share their audio reflection stories with other neighborhood families, visualize these stories on neighborhood maps, and listen to the stories while also viewing associated metadata about the story creators (e.g., the number of children in the family, average number of steps taken, etc.). Through a study evaluating Storywell 2, we demonstrated how technology-supported storytelling about past physical activity experiences can support self-modeling (i.e., learning from one?s past experiences), and how sharing these reflective stories with other families can support social modeling (i.e., learning from others? experiences). This work further showed how such digitally-supported modeling can positively impact physical activity self-efficacy and outcome expectations. 

Our studies have made scientific contributions through results demonstrating how story-scaffolded and data-driven reflection can support positive outcomes (e.g., increased self-efficacy) and engagement with mHealth tools within low-SES families. This work has also made theoretical contributions, by applying Self-Determination Theory and Social-Cognitive Theory in the context of health technology design for families. Through analyses of data across our studies, our work extends these theories, demonstrating how they can help support the creation of systems that families are motivated to use, that provide value to them (e.g., by addressing psychological needs and aspirations for their families), and that effectively support positive health behaviors (e.g., through the development of psychological attitudes that predict behavior change). 

Furthermore, our work suggests that community stories are an asset that communities can use to promote wellness. Within Social Cognitive Theory, social modeling is more effective when the model is perceived as similar by the observer. Thus, because our Storywell 2 participants shared similar life experiences and identities with one another, we found that the health behavior strategies conveyed through the stories are promising assets for social modeling and, ultimately, for health behavior promotion. This perspective?that stories are community assets--could further motivate future work in human-computer interaction to investigate how novel tools can support even more effective community storytelling. 

This work has been widely disseminated, through several publications--one of which received a best paper honorable mention award--a PhD dissertation, invited talks in diverse scholarly venues, and through presentation of this work to community partners. This work has also had broader impact. First, we released the Storywell app via an open-source license and created an open source API for retrieving and storing sensor-collected data directly from fitness tracking devices for individual users and social groups such as families. By making this software freely available, our work is helping to catalyze future digital health innovation. Additionally, educational contributions have been made through the mentorship and training of several graduate and undergraduate students, including many from groups underrepresented in computing, and the development and use of new digital health curricula. Lastly, this work demonstrates how experiential learning technologies can be an engaging and accessible approach to developing health literacy and behaviors that can help prevent the onset of diseases such as obesity and diabetes in low-SES families, who disproportionately experience these health challenges.

abstractText:
Variability in the transport of heat, freshwater and mass in the North Atlantic has been linked to a number of societally relevant factors including sea level change, the melting of sea and glacial ice, and anthropogenic carbon storage in the deep ocean. However, the current understanding of the drivers of such changes is limited, making an investigation of overturning in the Sub-polar region a key ocean research priority. This field program explicitly addresses this gap. Furthermore, by engaging the larger international community studying the North Atlantic, Overturning in the Sub-polar North Atlantic Program (OSNAP) is playing a key role in catalyzing scientific progress by promoting international collaborations, synthesis, and the sharing of resources and by training future generations. Key to the latter is a network of early career scientists whose professional growth will continue to be facilitated through targeted activities that have been tested and improved during OSNAP's initial phase. Graduate students and post-docs will be trained in seagoing operations and in the processing and analysis of observational data.

The overall goal of this field project, in conjunction with other measurements in the North Atlantic, is to establish determination of the linkage between intermediate and deep water formation and the overturning circulation--a connection that is present in climate models, but has yet to be observed. This project will also provide the first comprehensive view of spreading pathways for the deep waters in the Sub-polar basin. Starting in 2014, the US-led international project, Overturning in the Sub-polar North Atlantic Program (OSNAP), provides a continuous record of the full-water column, trans-basin fluxes of heat, mass and freshwater in the Sub-polar North Atlantic, in partnership with the UK, Netherlands, Canada, Germany and China. Data from the first 21 months of the full OSNAP observing system has been used to produce an initial time series of the meridional overturning, heat and freshwater fluxes for the Sub-polar basin. These preliminary results reveal a highly variable overturning in the basin, interior pathways for overflow waters, surprisingly energetic boundary current systems on timescales from days to months, and a strong overflow plume in the Iceland Basin. The additional two years of OSNAP observations will cover a time frame sufficient to make comparisons with other overturning time series and optimize the OSNAP measurement system--all necessary tasks prior to a request for longer term measurements. This component of OSNAP (OSNAP East) is for the eastern array between Greenland and Scotland in coordination with the UK and the Netherlands. The US contribution includes the East Greenland inshore and offshore arrays, the Iceland Basin array, and the integration of all OSNAP measurements. The sub-goal for OSNAP East is to quantify the structure and transport of the boundary currents off the east coast of Greenland and within the Iceland Basin, as well as determine their variability and forcing mechanisms.

projectOutComesReport:
To provide an observational basis for the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change projections of a slowing Atlantic meridional overturning circulation (MOC) in the 21st century, the Overturning in the Subpolar North Atlantic Program (OSNAP) observing system was launched in the summer of 2014. The first six years of the OSNAP observational record has revealed a highly variable overturning circulation responsible for the majority of the heat and freshwater transport across the OSNAP line. In a departure from the prevailing view that changes in deep water formation in the Labrador Sea dominate MOC variability, these results suggest that the conversion of warm, salty, shallow Atlantic waters into colder, fresher, deep waters that move southward in the Irminger and Iceland basins is largely responsible for overturning and its variability in the subpolar basin.

Furthermore, these OSNAP observations have revealed that changes in the western boundary current in the subpolar North Atlantic are not, by themselves, indicators of subpolar overturning variability on monthly to interannual time scales. The overturning lower limb in the subpolar North Atlantic has a complex circulation and changes in the full set of pathways combine to describe the MOC and its variability. Thus, a partial measurement of the deep western boundary current transport or density variations in a limited geographical area (e.g., in the central Labrador Sea or within the Labrador Sea western boundary) is insufficient to reconstruct MOC changes in the subpolar region on these time scales.

These results have implications for our interpretation of past climate changes and for our prediction of future climate changes.  As for the former, past reconstructions of MOC variability have relied on estimates of temperature and/or density anomalies along the western boundary in the North Atlantic.  Coupled with previous studies that have showed interior pathways for the transit of newly-formed deep waters to move equatorward, the OSNAP results indicate that anomalies along a western boundary are not synonymous with overturning variability.  Though the observational periods to date is six years, the mechanisms responsible for the decoupling of overturning variability and boundary density variability is expected to hold on longer time scale.

In a warming climate, a slowing of the overturning circulation Is expected due to the freshening and warming of the surface waters in the convection regions. Understanding where the majority of the deep water is currently formed in the subpolar North Atlantic aids our ability to predict the magnitude and pace of an expected slowdown. Because we now understand the sensitivity of the overturning variability to surface property changes in the Iceland and Irminger basins, we are able to focus monitoring and modeling efforts in that region.

projectOutComesReport:
The ocean's meridional overturning circulation (MOC) is a key component of the global climate system. The MOC, characterized in the Atlantic by a northward flow of warm upper-ocean waters and a compensating southward flow of cool deep waters, plays a fundamental role in establishing the mean climate and its variability on interannual to longer time scales. The heat carried northward as part of the upper MOC limb keeps the Northern Hemisphere generally, and western Europe in particular, warmer than they would be otherwise. Variations in the strength of the MOC are believed to influence North Atlantic sea surface temperatures, leading to impacts on rainfall over the African Sahel, India, and Brazil; Atlantic hurricane activity; and summer climate over Europe and North America. Finally, variability of the inflow of warm Atlantic waters into high latitudes has been linked to the decline of Arctic sea ice and mass loss from the Greenland Ice Sheet, both of which have profound consequences for climate variability.

Though less studied than its impact on climate, the MOC?s role in the ocean carbon cycle has emerged as a recent concern. The North Atlantic is a strong sink for atmospheric carbon dioxide, accounting for ~40% of the annual mean uptake of carbon dioxide across the air?sea interface, with nearly half of that uptake occurring north of 50?N. Furthermore, modeling and observational studies show that the North Atlantic plays a crucial role in the uptake of anthropogenic carbon. 

Given the imperative of understanding MOC variability and based on recommendations of the ocean science community, an international team of oceanographer, led by NSF-funded US PIs, developed an observing system for sustained transbasin measurements in the subpolar North Atlantic, called Overturning in the Subpolar North Atlantic Program (OSNAP). Deployed in the summer of 2014, OSNAP is measuring the full-depth transport of water associated with the AMOC as well as meridional heat and freshwater transport. The first 21-month record from this time series produced a ?sea change? in our understanding of the MOC.  In a departure from the prevailing view that changes in the deep water formation in the Labrador Sea dominate MOC variability, the first OSNAP results suggest that the conversion of warm, salty and shallow Atlantic waters into colder, fresher and deeper waters that move southward in the Irminger and Iceland basins is largely responsible for the overturning and its variability in the subpolar basin.

This result is important to oceanographers since we now understand where to focus our observational efforts and how to interpret the signals of downstream MOC variability.  This result is important to climate scientists since we now have a better understanding of what drives MOC variability and where to look for surface property changes, such as warming and freshening, that will impact local convection and MOC variability.  The overall goal is to understand MOC variability in order to improve model projections of our future climate.

The Overturning in the Subpolar North Atlantic Program (OSNAP) also deployed 135 acoustically-tracked deep floats to track the spreading pathways of Iceland-Scotland Overflow Water (ISOW) and Denmark Strait Overflow Water (DSOW) from 2014 to 2018. These water masses, which originate in the Nordic Seas, are transported by the deepest branch of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC). The OSNAP floats provide the first directly-observed, comprehensive view of ISOW and DSOW spreading pathways throughout the subpolar North Atlantic. The collection of OSNAP float trajectories, complemented by model simulations, reveals that their pathways are not restricted to western boundary currents, and they are remarkably different from each other in character. The spread of DSOW from the Irminger Sea is primarily via the swift deep boundary currents of the Irminger and Labrador Seas, whereas the spread of ISOW out of the Iceland Basin is slower and along multiple export pathways. The characterization of these Overflow Water pathways has important implications for our understanding of the AMOC and its variability. Finally, reconstructions of AMOC variability from proxy data, involving either the strength of boundary currents and/or the property variability of deep waters, should account for the myriad pathways of DSOW and ISOW, but particularly so for the latter.

title: Collaborative Research: Overturning in the Subpolar North Atlantic - Labrador Basin and Floats

abstractText:
This project is one of two components of a US-led international program, Overturning in the Sub-polar North Atlantic (OSNAP), designed to provide a continuous record of the full-water column, trans-basin fluxes of heat, mass and freshwater in the subpolar North Atlantic. The OSNAP observing system consists of two legs: one extending from southern Labrador to the southwestern tip of Greenland across the mouth of the Labrador Sea (OSNAP West), and the second from the southeastern tip of Greenland to Scotland (OSNAP East). The observing system also includes subsurface floats (OSNAP Floats) in order to trace the pathways of overflow waters in the basin and to assess the connectivity of currents crossing the OSNAP line. The location of the OSNAP East and West legs purposefully melds with a number of long-term observational efforts in the North Atlantic: the Canadian repeat hydrography program in the Labrador Sea; the German Labrador Sea western boundary array at 53°N; the global Ocean Observatories Initiative node to be placed in the southwestern Irminger Sea; the repeat hydrographic sections across the Irminger and Iceland basins; and the Ellett line in the Rockall region. Substantial international collaboration has been garnered for OSNAP, including measurement contributions from the UK, Germany, the Netherlands and Canada. Importantly, this proposed observing system, in conjunction with the RAPID/MOCHA array at 26°N and the European Union NACLIM program at Nordic Seas overflows, will provide the first comprehensive three-dimensional measure of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) and provide a means to evaluate inter-gyre connectivity in the North Atlantic. 

This collaborative project will implement the OSNAP West  section and the OSNAP Float program. The primary observational components are: (i) a mooring array across the eastern margin of the Labrador Sea, where the subpolar boundary current enters the basin. This array will complement an analogous array across the western margin at the exit point of the Labrador Sea, maintained by institutions in Germany and Canada; (ii) a sequential release of acoustically tracked floats in the lower limb of the AMOC at the OSNAP East and OSNAP West boundary arrays. These floats will be seeded in the two densest components of North Atlantic Deep Water (NADW) over the four-year period of the measurement program (2014-2018).

Intellectual Merit: For decades oceanographers have understood the AMOC to be highly susceptible to changes in the production of NADW. However, a number of recent observational and modeling studies have called into question this supposition, as more has been learned about the role of wind forcing in AMOC variability. Thus, the overall goal of this project is to establish an observing system that will determine the role that intermediate and deep water mass formation and basin-scale wind forcing play in the overturning and associated poleward heat transport, assessments that currently have only been theorized and modeled, but not observed.

Broader Impact: In January of 2007, the US Joint Subcommittee on Ocean Science and Technology identified the study of the AMOC as one of four near-term priorities in the US Ocean Research Priorities Plan. This proposed work directly addresses that priority via a design of an AMOC observing system in the sub-polar North Atlantic. While a primary motivation for studying AMOC variability comes from its potential impact on the climate system, additional motivation for the measure of the heat, mass and freshwater fluxes in the sub-polar North Atlantic arises from their potential impact on marine biogeochemistry and the cryosphere. There is growing evidence that the ocean has played (and is playing) a role in the reduction of Arctic sea ice and in mass loss from the Greenland Ice Sheet - both of which have been attributed to changes in the poleward heat transport by the ocean. Also, the ocean plays an essential role in the carbon cycle by moderating increasing atmospheric concentrations of CO2 through the sequestration of anthropogenic carbon in the deep ocean. Variability in the AMOC is expected to impact this sequestration. Broader impacts also include the training of five graduate students in seagoing operations and in the processing and analysis of observational data. The graduate students will have an opportunity to collaborate with their international counterparts through virtual meetings and in-person visits and will be mentored by multiple advisors.
 
This research award includes support for a Science Across Virtual Institutes (SAVI) that is co-funded by NSF's Office of International and Integrative Activities.

projectOutComesReport:
Oceanographers have been concerned with how ocean currents transport heat and carbon from one part of the world to another for many decades.  One current system in particular has been of primary interest, namely the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC), as its variability has been conjectured to have strong impacts on sea surface temperatures in the North Atlantic, which in turn influence rainfall over the African Sahel, India and Brazil, Atlantic hurricane activity and summer climate over Europe and North America. Additional motivation for the measure of the AMOC arises from its potential impact on marine biogeochemistry and the cryosphere. There is growing evidence that the ocean has played, and is playing, a role in the reduction of Arctic sea ice and in mass loss from the Greenland Ice Sheet – both of which have been attributed to changes in the poleward heat transport by the ocean. Also, the ocean plays an essential role in the carbon cycle by moderating increasing atmospheric concentrations of carbon dioxide through the sequestration of anthropogenic carbon in the deep ocean.

A US-led international effort, Overturning in the Subpolar North Atlantic Program (OSNAP), was initiated in 2014 to directly measure the AMOC at subpolar latitudes in the North Atlantic in order to understand its magnitude, its variability and what causes it to change from year to year.  The OSNAP array has provided a continuous record of the full-water column, trans-basin fluxes of heat, mass, and freshwater in the subpolar North Atlantic since its deployment, in partnership with the UK, Netherlands, France, China, Canada and Germany. The first four years of data from the OSNAP observing system have shown that the eastern subpolar region, from Greenland to Scotland, dominates the overturning in the subpolar North Atlantic, a result that has challenged the current understanding of overturning in the subpolar North Atlantic, which has largely been based on climate models. The new results from OSNAP also show that deep waters from the Nordic Seas take unexpected pathways as they flow southward into the subtropical region of the North Atlantic.  Finally, with the measure of the AMOC and its variability in the subpolar North Atlantic, oceanographers now have a better understanding of how atmospheric forcing and the underlying sea surface conditions impact the AMOC magnitude from year to year.  This understanding will help us, in the years to come, to 1) analyze the extent to which the flow of warm waters associated with the AMOC impacts the decline of Arctic sea-ice and mass loss from the Greenland Ice Sheet; 2) improve prediction capabilities for North Atlantic sea surface temperatures; 3) understand the extent to which the expected increase in freshwater transport into the subpolar North Atlantic will affect AMOC variability and 4) assess where and how we should monitor the AMOC variability in the decades ahead.
